taxonomyNote: NatureServe (Burbrink 2002) restricts P. guttatus to east of the Mississippi River and treats the Great Plains rat snake as P. emoryi and western Louisiana/eastern Texas populations as P. slowinskii; Animal Diversity Web still lists P. g. emoryi as a subspecies and covers it in this species' range.
fieldMarks: Large spots down the back, brown and red-orange body (gray and yellow variants occur), belly with a black-and-white checkerboard.
Hatchlings paler and duller, 20-35 cm; adults average 70-120 cm.
Head narrower than a copperhead's, colour lighter, and spots square-shaped.
behavior: Mostly diurnal, crepuscular in warm weather; climbs trees and shrubs, basks on rocks, enters rodent burrows; constricts prey.
Over half the diet is rodents (hispid cotton rats, white-footed mice) plus moles, bird eggs, and lizards and frogs in Florida.
Hibernates in crevices, logs or caves from about October to April in most of the range, briefly or not at all in the south.
habitat: Pine woodlands, brushy fields, open hardwood forests, rocky areas with crevices and logs, fields, barnyards and abandoned buildings; up to about 1800 m.
range: Southeastern United States from southern New Jersey to Florida and west through Mississippi to Louisiana; related Great Plains rat snake reaches Illinois, Texas and New Mexico. Not in Canada.

lookalikes.name: Southern copperhead
lookalikes.howToTell: Corn snake has a narrower head, lighter coloration and square spots.
